metadata.title: Exploring Information Behavior with Hierarchical Goal Decomposition: The Case of a Web-Based Consumer-Oriented Genetics Resource
metadata.abstract_summary: Hospital libraries must design their Websites to effectively serve patrons’ information needs. Usability testing is a validated method of evaluating a library’s Website design.

Hierarchical Goal Decomposition (HGD) provides a means to leverage a user’s knowledge base or augment a deficit of knowledge to achieve a fruitful experience at the hospital’s Website. This paper docu- ments the use of HGD to analyze Genetic Home Reference, a resource available through the National Library of Medicine. Through this work, this paper provides guidelines for individual hospital librarians to utilize HGD to inform Website design for a hospital or hospital library Website. Although labor-intensive, HGD can provide information of a high de- gree of granularity with a smaller sample size that delivers high qual- ity information. doi:10.1300/J186v07n02_09 [Article copies available for a fee from The Haworth Document Delivery Service: 1-800-HAWORTH. sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Hospital library Websites are now becoming a commonly implement- ed means of providing access to health information. The library Website delivers valuable health information in a digital format via electronic journals, reference resources, research tools, and electronic books. Hos- pital libraries must design their Websites to effectively serve patrons’ in- formation needs (1). Usability testing is a validated method of evaluating a library’s Website design (2). Usability testing enables the opportunity to observe and evaluate real-world Website navigation. The goal of test- ing is to reveal usability problems and thus improve Website design (3). Valuable information about the effectiveness of Website design can be gained by observing relatively few Website users (4). The diversity of patrons that hospital libraries serve, from consumers to clinicians to hospital administrators, requires an even greater degree of Website design effectiveness. Consumers will vary widely in the pro- cedural knowledge they bring in performing Web navigational tasks. These users may bring a lower degree of subject matter knowledge, in contrast to clinician users, who will exhibit a high degree of this domain knowledge. Both groups may have variable degrees of procedural knowledge in navigating electronic resources. The hospital librarian will have to design the Website to make the best use of this variety of knowledge background. The need to address this wide variety of poten- tial users in Website design may increase the need for usability testing. Possible challenges exist for the hospital librarian to implement usabil- ity studies. Securing a representative sample of the range of potential users to participate in testing may be challenging. In addition, some of the more specific needs of usability testing, such as a testing room, video equipment, user logs, and the time and personnel needed to observe and analyze navigation behavior, may be unavailable.

sections.heading: METHODS
sections.text: Hierarchical Goal Decomposition (HGD) works by comparing expert and novice behavior. Hospital librarians can utilize their own expert be- havior coupled with assistance of domain experts to create an expert model. Novice models will be constructed as a result of observational and think-aloud studies. By comparing these two models, a type of gap analy- sis will emerge to inform Website design leveraging current knowledge and augmenting knowledge deficits to provide an efficient and fruitful Website experience. Looking at user behavior as a series of tasks performed in a contin- uum of abstraction, descriptions of the tasks can be depicted at different levels of detail. HGD is an analysis tool that decomposes higher-level abstract tasks such as cognition into progressively lower-level concrete steps and articulates the declarative and procedural knowledge that is needed to successfully complete the task at each level (5). The analytic approach is to make the implicit–how people solve problems in the cog- nitive space–explicit, by providing a visual diagram and lists of discrete steps that represent cognition and knowledge involved in the task. This depiction makes the interactions between cognitive styles and aspects of information behavior more readily discoverable than other analytic approaches, and resource design can be informed to more effectively respond to the users’ information needs (6). HGD works by comparing expert and novice models. Consistent patterns of user behavior in navi- gation and similar gaps in knowledge can be found providing a model for analysis that represents information-processing needs at a high degree of granularity. HGD has its genesis in task analysis, a structured way of breaking down a complex behavior into its component parts (5). By looking at a task as a sequential hierarchical series of sub-tasks, a greater level of de- tail can be uncovered. HGD relies on elements of the GOMS model Technology 93 describing the knowledge that a user must have in order to carry out tasks (7, 8). HGD works by looking at an “expert” user’s behavior and procedural and domain knowledge levels required to complete the task. The “expert” or experienced user serves as a model in comparing the be- havior and knowledge levels of a “novice” or inexperienced user. As seen in Figure 1, the HGD framework will result in a four-layered four-columned model. This model is formed from a task performed on Genetic Home Reference. Debuting in April 2003, the Genetics Home Reference (GHR) is the National Library of Medicine’s Website for consumer information about genetic conditions and the genes responsi- ble for those conditions. The site was designed to provide information to consumers with a basic understanding of science, defined as those in- dividuals who had completed a high school or college freshmen-level biology course. Broadly, the left side of the model shows the hierarchical goal de- composition of the task with the right layer showing the declarative and procedural knowledge needed at each level of the decomposition. The center of the model contains the names of the four layers of knowledge in the goal decomposition: Task, intermediate, command, and keystroke. Moving from top to bottom: 1. Task layer , the highest level of abstraction, describes the task to be performed 2. Intermediate layer , beginning to focus, decomposes the task with the procedural and declarative knowledge needed to organize the different kinds of commands provided by the system 3. Command layer increases the focus of the decomposition on each of the stages in the intermediate layer into specific commands 4. Keystroke layer , the most concrete layer decomposes the task into specific tasks needed to accomplish the command (5). Declarative knowledge is the factual and relationship knowledge needed to negotiate the site. This could also be called the domain knowledge. Expert Model of Task to “Is There Gene Therapy Available for Disease?” 95 In using HGD to examine usability, one should choose tasks that are representative of typical uses of the resource as well as the intended use of the resource. Tasks should take advantage of the features built in the resource and have varying levels of complexity and ease. Tasks should not be so time consuming as to tire or confuse users (9). To construct an HGD model, a source, tasks, users, and experts must be chosen. Tasks should be representative of tasks the user would per- form. Two HGD models must be constructed. One model should illus- trate the behavior of the expert providing the ideal of behavior and knowledge to perform the selected task. Novice models must be con- structed for each user providing a replication of user behavior and stated comments. As the behavior is analyzed, the knowledge gaps may be either verbalized by the user or inferred or uncovered by the observer. It is in the side-by-side comparison that the gaps of knowledge become apparent. Empirical usability evaluation methods, which encompass most vari- eties of user testing, measure performance directly while analytic meth- ods examine the interface, aspects of the interaction and infer usability problems (10). Empirical usability methods such as log analysis, key- stroke analysis, and transactional log analysis can provide rich data on user behavior, system, and user interface performance and effi- ciency. Information can be gleaned regarding usage of the system, clues to efficiency of a system or a user interface, type and number of failure rates, total number of searches, the structure, number, length, and time of queries or user input number and type of results, highlight the time the system or particular area was used and with IP address can even gauge user characteristics and demographics (11, 12, 13). Log analysis gives a strong system perspective. It can be objective providing data on time spent at certain areas, the number of keystrokes or keyboard activ- ity to perform a task. User intention or thought has to be inferred. While empirical methods measure productivity, the factors affecting user be- havior satisfaction can only be inferred. Analytic methods attempt to make predictions concerning payoff performance. Methods such as walkthroughs, guidelines, interactive and heuristic evaluations are examples of analytical methods. Analytic methods are particularly indicated when wanting to examine user be- havior in conjunction with an interface or system. A powerful feature of analytic usability methods is the focused examination of intrinsic attrib- utes of both users and interfaces and attempts to recreate or describe their behavior (10). Additional features of analytical methods are the emphasis on knowledge-based behavior or learning. The number and 96

sections.text: type of subjects in analytical methods differ from the subjects in empiri- cal methods. Indeed in empirical methods, users tend to be represented objectively and in large numbers, while with analytic methods the subject pool tends to be small and the data are represented qualitatively rather than quantitatively (9, 11, 12, 13). In analytical methods the goal is to re- create an ideal user experience by representing as closely as possible the intended user a system or interface is being designed for (14). To determine representative tasks, a structured approach should be used. A log analysis can provide information regarding usage of the sys- tem and will aid in developing appropriate tasks. Tasks should be writ- ten in a vignette style to provide context for the user. Combining all the information gathered should result in a small set of representative tasks. The tasks should be tested with a small user group for understandability and ability of the site to answer the questions. Based on the feedback, the tasks can be fine-tuned and finalized. As tasks are to be typical of the site, users also should be representa- tive of intended users. In the case of utilizing HGD for this project, key individuals in the development of the site were interviewed. To deter- mine the intended user, the technical and content staff was interviewed. Dr. Joyce Mitchell, project lead, offered information detailing the impe- tus of the creation and mission of the site. Content developers were in- terviewed to determine the type of user that was envisioned and the level at which the content was written. Technical staff offered insights into the development of the algorithm and nuts and bolts functioning of the site. Based on this information, it was determined that the site was geared toward those individuals with a freshmen college level or high school biology class. It was also expected that the typical user might be a newly diagnosed individual or have a family member who had been diagnosed with a genetic condition. For the hospital librarian who may also be the developer, the information for the intended user may be much more accessible. It would be wise to include all interested parties, however, in determining the intended user. Since HGD compares novice users with expert users, an expert or ex- perienced user was needed. Ideally the expert should possess both pro- cedural and domain knowledge. In the case of preparing an HGD model that serves as the basis of this paper, a medical librarian was chosen to serve as the expert in procedural knowledge of the site. A medical li- brarian possesses the domain knowledge of searching and procedural knowledge of the site’s format, content, and structure. It is appropriate to combine experts in domain and procedural knowledge to construct an expert model. The model is not limited to the behavior of one individual Technology 97 but an amalgam of expert behavior. Novice models will be constructed as the result of the analysis of the behavior of the study subjects. It is in the comparison of these two models that a type of gap analysis will emerge. Users without strong scientific knowledge and those that did not per- form formalized Web searching were chosen from employees at Lister Hill. User behavior was captured by videotaping screen behavior and voice. Thinking aloud was encouraged to uncover the cognition of the user. As each user moved through the set of tasks, the observer re- mained beside the user offering only neutral comments and prompting the user for verbal feedback as users decreased their verbalizations. The observer had a blank HGD model to begin sketching out initial thoughts and to note anything of immediate interest. As each session ended, the observer watched the tapes again noting comments and having the ad- vantage to slow or stop the tape to minutely observe behaviors. Users were given consent forms and offered the opportunity to leave the study at any time.

sections.heading: RESULTS
sections.text: Qualitative studies yield rich and copious amounts of data; however, for this particular use of HGD, no automated method of analyzing the data was used. There are many methods now available to facilitate the analysis of qualitative data. It is beyond the scope of this paper to ex- plore or comment on qualitative data analysis. User HGD models were grouped by task and analysis began by manually inspecting each com- pleted model. Notes were kept for each user and similarities begun to emerge quickly. Users consistently used either search or browse to ac- complish the task with a browse rate of 28%. Every user consistently avoided the left hand side of the GHR site. Narrative material in the dis- play results was ignored. Users articulated different expectations for displayed information.

sections.text: or question (15). To be useful, comparison studies must be done that de- lineate the advantages and disadvantages of each technique. HGD optimizes the advantages of both analytic and empirical methods of us- ability techniques. By focusing not only on the task but also on the con- comitant needed knowledge, a fuller picture of the user experience is captured. In usability, doing something is better than doing nothing; however, different techniques identify different problems rendering compari- sons of results of different usability evaluation ambiguous and confusing (16, 10). HGD is useful because it is the combination of the analytical and empirical that allows simultaneous comparisons of behavior and cogni- tion. The analytic approach is to make the implicit (i.e., how people solve problems in the cognitive space), explicit by providing a visual diagram and lists of discrete steps that represent cognition and knowledge in- volved in the task. It is the unique combining of knowledge and task lay- ers that allow a holistic picture of user behavior. It has been shown that fewer numbers of users can provide legitimate results. About 50% of users are search-dominant, while 20% are link- dominant and the rest are mixed-dominant (16). The users in this study had a 28% browse rate that greatly mirrors those results. Fewer users can identify problems and fewer still can identify major problems. Three to five users have been said to produce reliable results (16). Test- ing five people three times yields more information than fifteen people (17). HGD can be a daunting analysis tool for the first time, but the abil- ity to realize reliable results makes the work worthwhile. By comparing the two models of expert and novice behavior, gaps in knowledge or skill can be discovered. HGD leverages the power of the user to articulate and describe their interaction with a resource. Video- taping allowed screen behavior and voice to be captured. Thinking aloud captures cognition by having users verbalize what they are think- ing. While users may not articulate exactly what they are thinking or may even self-censor, use of both of these techniques can give an ap- proximation of what is thought. What is said and what is happening may not be the same. For example, people may say they are typing in one term but actually may be misspelling the term. Use of both of these tech- niques may capture any mismatches. While videotaping may seem daunting, it can be quite simple. The videotape only captures voice, screen, and keyboard behavior. The user is never viewed. Unlike other usability techniques, HGD has the unique ability to cap- ture the knowledge layers of a task. Knowledge is an important compo- nent of user behavior that is often ignored. The ability to understand the Technology 99 impact of knowledge can explain why a complex task is difficult to ac- quire despite years of experience using resources (5). Examination of strategy alone is not sufficient (5). It does not fully explain why strategies are not spontaneously acquired from the knowledge of the tool or the tasks. HGD combines the task and the knowledge to provide a deeper under- standing and also by decomposing and identifying and differentiating between the strategy and the knowledge, the level of knowledge can be controlled to allow for testing of hypothesis (5).

sections.heading: CONCLUSION
sections.text: HGD is a labor-intensive process that uncovers powerful and unique combinations of data not replicated with other analytical techniques. HGD provides a model to allow for analysis of behavior that will rap- idly and accurately allow development of more usable sites. The future for HGD lies in its ability to be used in the analysis of many of the com- plex information situations while maintaining a manageable investment of time and labor by the hospital librarian.
